description: Emergency POCUS interpretation corpus for the Clinical Reasoning Agent. Thirty knowledge units, each answering one clinical question, rather than thirty documents.
scope_note: Clinical knowledge only. Laboratory reference ranges are deliberately NOT here: comparing a value against a threshold is deterministic, and clinical_state.py already does it, printing e.g. 'bnp: 890.0 pg/mL <-- HIGH (ref <=100)'. Putting the same information in a retrieval corpus would make a settled comparison depend on a similarity score.
licence_note: Store a citation and a short quotation per unit. Do NOT redistribute whole guideline documents: most are copyrighted. Every unit must name where its text came from before it is used for anything reported.
how_to_use: Replace each unit whose status is 'placeholder' with real text and a real citation, then set status to 'sourced'. Retrieval returns placeholders so the pipeline is testable before real content exists, but reason() marks any answer resting on them as NOT guideline-grounded, so a placeholder can never pass as evidence.

passages.source: Murali A, Prakash A, Dixit R, Juneja M, Kumar N. Lung ultrasound for evaluation of dyspnea: a pictorial review. Acute Crit Care. 2022;37(4):502-15. doi:10.4266/acc.2022.00780 (CC BY-NC 4.0)
passages.text: The presence of three or more B-lines in one longitudinal scan, disseminated to the anterior chest wall bilaterally with preserved lung sliding, is called the B-profile. A B-line is a comet-tail artifact that always arises from the pleural line, always moves in synchrony with lung sliding, is almost always long and spreads out to the edge of the screen without fading, and almost always erases A-lines. Diffuse interstitial syndrome is an ultrasound diagnosis defined by the presence of multiple (three or more) B-lines in more than one scanning zone in the anterolateral chest wall, bilaterally; a few B-lines may be normally seen in basal lung zones.

passages.source: Murali A, Prakash A, Dixit R, Juneja M, Kumar N. Lung ultrasound for evaluation of dyspnea: a pictorial review. Acute Crit Care. 2022;37(4):502-15. doi:10.4266/acc.2022.00780 (CC BY-NC 4.0)
passages.text: In the critically ill, diffuse interstitial syndrome is almost always due to pulmonary edema, either hemodynamic (fluid overload or cardiogenic) or permeability induced (acute respiratory distress syndrome, post-infectious, and similar). The appearance of the pleural line can be used as a criterion to differentiate pulmonary edema from interstitial lung disease, with a regular pleural line seen in pulmonary edema; criteria described for pulmonary fibrosis include irregularity, tightening, fragmentation, blurring and thickening of the pleural line. A homogeneous, diffuse distribution of B-lines is seen in pulmonary edema, in contrast to a non-homogeneous distribution with areas of sparing noted in ARDS or acute lung injury.

passages.source: Murali A, Prakash A, Dixit R, Juneja M, Kumar N. Lung ultrasound for evaluation of dyspnea: a pictorial review. Acute Crit Care. 2022;37(4):502-15. doi:10.4266/acc.2022.00780 (CC BY-NC 4.0)
passages.text: When two reflective parallel interfaces lie in the path of the ultrasound beam, the beam gets reflected multiple times between these interfaces, generating an image comprising multiple echogenic parallel lines placed equidistant from each other, which decrease in brightness with increasing depth. In the chest, the pleural line lies parallel to the probe and acts as a reflective interface when the lungs are aerated, giving rise to reverberation artifacts known as A-lines. Hence, the presence of A-lines denotes an aerated lung.

passages.source: Murali A, Prakash A, Dixit R, Juneja M, Kumar N. Lung ultrasound for evaluation of dyspnea: a pictorial review. Acute Crit Care. 2022;37(4):502-15. doi:10.4266/acc.2022.00780 (CC BY-NC 4.0)
passages.text: The A-profile is defined by the presence of both lung sliding and A-lines on anterior scans, bilaterally. Sometimes one or two B-lines with lung sliding may also be seen and are also included under the A-profile. The normal physiological movement of the lungs results in sliding of the visceral pleura against the motionless parietal pleura, resulting in a twinkling, to-and-fro motion called lung sliding; on M-mode the seashore sign is demonstrated, in which the motionless portion of the chest above the pleural line creates horizontal waves and the lung sliding below the pleural line creates a granular pattern, the sand.

passages.source: Murali A, Prakash A, Dixit R, Juneja M, Kumar N. Lung ultrasound for evaluation of dyspnea: a pictorial review. Acute Crit Care. 2022;37(4):502-15. doi:10.4266/acc.2022.00780 (CC BY-NC 4.0)
passages.text: The A'-profile is defined by abolished lung sliding at the anterior chest wall with the A-line sign. The presence of air between the parietal and visceral pleura in the case of pneumothorax results in a lack of lung sliding; this is further confirmed using the M-mode tracing, which will display horizontal lines above and below the pleural line, known as the barcode or stratosphere sign. The A-line sign refers to a pattern of exclusive A-lines with a complete absence of B-lines, the loss of B-lines being a result of air accumulating within the pleural space, eliminating the acoustic impedance gradient and thereby hindering the propagation of sound waves.

passages.source: Murali A, Prakash A, Dixit R, Juneja M, Kumar N. Lung ultrasound for evaluation of dyspnea: a pictorial review. Acute Crit Care. 2022;37(4):502-15. doi:10.4266/acc.2022.00780 (CC BY-NC 4.0)
passages.text: After establishing the A' profile, the next step to confirm the diagnosis of pneumothorax is to detect the lung point sign, which occurs at the border of the pneumothorax due to the sliding lung intermittently coming into contact with the chest wall during inspiration. On M-mode this sign is translated as alternating seashore and stratosphere patterns appearing over time when the probe is kept at a particular location, and the more lateral or posterior the lung point sign is identified, the larger the pneumothorax. The lung point sign is 100% specific for pneumothorax but has a relatively low sensitivity of 66%, and is not seen in cases of total lung collapse.

passages.source: Murali A, Prakash A, Dixit R, Juneja M, Kumar N. Lung ultrasound for evaluation of dyspnea: a pictorial review. Acute Crit Care. 2022;37(4):502-15. doi:10.4266/acc.2022.00780 (CC BY-NC 4.0)
passages.text: In the BLUE protocol, the terms used for lung consolidation are pneumonia for anterior consolidation and posterolateral alveolar and/or pleural syndrome (PLAPS) for consolidation and/or pleural effusion in posterolateral lung zones. Anterior consolidation is designated a C-profile, while posterolateral consolidation in a patient showing A-profile anteriorly is designated an A-no V-PLAPS profile; unilateral lung rockets are designated A/B profile, and diffuse bilateral B-lines with loss of lung sliding a B' profile. Four patterns of consolidation were described to diagnose pneumonia: non-translobar consolidation, translobar consolidation, small subpleural consolidation identified by a C-line, and the unilateral lung rocket pattern. A shredded margin or frank hepatisation with sonographic bronchograms denotes underlying lung consolidation.

passages.source: Murali A, Prakash A, Dixit R, Juneja M, Kumar N. Lung ultrasound for evaluation of dyspnea: a pictorial review. Acute Crit Care. 2022;37(4):502-15. doi:10.4266/acc.2022.00780 (CC BY-NC 4.0)
passages.text: In the BLUE protocol the lung line, quad sign and sinusoid sign are described as criteria for diagnosis of pleural effusion, disregarding the echogenicity of the collection. The lung line is a regular line which outlines the effusion, indicating the visceral pleural line, roughly parallel to the pleural line, so that all effusions, anechoic or echoic, can be diagnosed using it; the quad sign refers to the rough quadrilateral appearance of the effusion framed by the pleural line superiorly, the visceral line inferiorly and rib shadows on either side. On M-mode, a sinusoidal pattern is noted due to movement of the lung line towards the motionless pleural line on inspiration and downward movement on expiration; this sign is specific for pleural effusion, however it is absent in very viscous or septate effusions.

passages.source: Murali A, Prakash A, Dixit R, Juneja M, Kumar N. Lung ultrasound for evaluation of dyspnea: a pictorial review. Acute Crit Care. 2022;37(4):502-15. doi:10.4266/acc.2022.00780 (CC BY-NC 4.0)
passages.text: Detection of the lung point confirms the diagnosis of pneumothorax; if the lung point is not demonstrated, the patient would require further diagnostic modalities for assessment. Lung sliding has been found to be absent in many cases other than pneumothorax, including pleural effusions, acute respiratory distress syndrome, large consolidations, pulmonary fibrosis, pleural adhesions, atelectasis, right mainstem intubation, and phrenic nerve paralysis. Thus, lung sliding when used alone has a low specificity.

passages.source: Murali A, Prakash A, Dixit R, Juneja M, Kumar N. Lung ultrasound for evaluation of dyspnea: a pictorial review. Acute Crit Care. 2022;37(4):502-15. doi:10.4266/acc.2022.00780 (CC BY-NC 4.0)
passages.text: One of the principles of lung ultrasound in the critically ill states that life-threatening disorders usually have an extensive projection. On this premise six BLUE-points were defined, much like the standard electrode placement in electrocardiography, allowing a simplified, quick and standardized technique for evaluating a critically ill patient at the bedside; on each side there are two points on the anterior chest wall (upper and lower BLUE point) and one located semi-posteriorly (the posterolateral alveolar and/or pleural syndrome, or PLAPS, point), which allows the detection of consolidation and/or pleural effusion. The BLUE protocol provides lung ultrasound profiles with an algorithmic approach to assist in diagnosis of six common acute conditions causing dyspnea: pneumothorax (A' profile), pneumonia (C profile, AB profile, B' profile and A-no V-PLAPS profile), pulmonary edema (B profile), acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or asthma (A-no V-no PLAPS profile), and pulmonary embolism (A-V profile).

passages.source: Albaroudi B, Haddad M, Albaroudi O, et al. Assessing left ventricular systolic function by emergency physician using point of care echocardiography compared to expert: systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur J Emerg Med. 2022;29(1):18-32. doi:10.1097/MEJ.0000000000000866 (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 -- sentences quoted verbatim and unaltered, as the licence forbids derivatives)
passages.text: Cardiac function was categorised as normal (ejection fraction >= 50%), reduced (ejection fraction 30-49%) or severely reduced (ejection fraction <30%) function. LVSF was ranked simply as normal or abnormal in two studies with cutoff ejection fraction value of 50%. Agreement between emergency physicians and experts gave a simple Kappa of 0.68 (95% confidence interval, 0.57-0.79). The overall quality of studies was low, with most being small, single centre convenience samples.

passages.source: Ha YR, Toh HC. Clinically integrated multi-organ point-of-care ultrasound for undifferentiated respiratory difficulty, chest pain, or shock: a critical analytic review. J Intensive Care. 2016;4:54. doi:10.1186/s40560-016-0172-1 (CC BY 4.0)
passages.text: An RV-to-LV end-diastolic diameter ratio greater than 0.9 was reported to indicate critical pulmonary embolism. The absence of sonographic signs of RV overload or dysfunction practically excludes pulmonary embolism as the cause of hemodynamic instability.

passages.source: Moura de Azevedo S, Duarte R, Krowicki J, Vazquez D, Pires Ferreira Arroja S, Mariz J. Heart in Focus: Advancing Pericardial Effusion Diagnosis With Point-of-Care Ultrasound. Cureus. 2024;16(12):e76681. doi:10.7759/cureus.76681 (CC BY 4.0)
passages.text: Pericardial effusion appears as an area without echoes between the heart and the outer layer of the pericardium on an echocardiogram. Effusions are graded by the echo-free space measured in diastole: a small effusion is less than 10 mm, corresponding to approximately 300 ml of fluid; a moderate effusion measures 10-20 mm, corresponding to approximately 500 ml; and a large effusion is greater than 20 mm, corresponding to approximately 700 ml.

passages.source: Moura de Azevedo S, Duarte R, Krowicki J, Vazquez D, Pires Ferreira Arroja S, Mariz J. Heart in Focus: Advancing Pericardial Effusion Diagnosis With Point-of-Care Ultrasound. Cureus. 2024;16(12):e76681. doi:10.7759/cureus.76681 (CC BY 4.0)
passages.text: The diastolic collapse of the right atrium is a significant echocardiographic finding in cardiac tamponade and is one of the earliest signs of the condition. While RV diastolic collapse is less sensitive than RA collapse for detecting tamponade, it is highly specific for the condition when it occurs. The IVC remains plethoric, with minimal respiratory variation; this sign is highly sensitive for tamponade (95-97%) with a valuable negative predictive value, but has lower specificity (approximately 40%). In certain clinical situations, such as in cases of RV hypertrophy or significantly elevated RV diastolic pressure (for example acute or chronic cor pulmonale), collapse of the right heart chambers may not be evident, even in the presence of tamponade.

passages.source: Ha YR, Toh HC. Clinically integrated multi-organ point-of-care ultrasound for undifferentiated respiratory difficulty, chest pain, or shock: a critical analytic review. J Intensive Care. 2016;4:54. doi:10.1186/s40560-016-0172-1 (CC BY 4.0)
passages.text: The priority is to rule out obstructive shock first, followed by cardiogenic shock, and then finally absolute or relative (distributive) hypovolemic shocks. Where the lung pattern is diffusely interstitial, cardiogenic shock is most likely. Where it is not, the findings are suggestive of obstructive or hypovolemic shock: IVC plethora indicates obstructive shock, while a small non-plethoric IVC is usually associated with hypovolemic shock.

passages.source: Savoia P, Jayanthi SK, Chammas MC. Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST). J Med Ultrasound. 2023;31(2):101-6. doi:10.4103/jmu.jmu_12_23 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 -- quoted verbatim and unaltered; ShareAlike binds derivatives, which a verbatim quotation is not)
passages.text: This should be the second FAST protocol region examined after confirming there is no hemopericardium. In the abdomen, it must be the first region examined because small amounts of hemoperitoneum may accumulate in there. The hepatorenal space, known as Morrison’s pouch, should be swept. Liquid in the perihepatic area should also be searched. Negative FAST is considered absolutely no fluid. Positive FAST is whether small or large amounts of fluid.

passages.source: Savoia P, Jayanthi SK, Chammas MC. Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST). J Med Ultrasound. 2023;31(2):101-6. doi:10.4103/jmu.jmu_12_23 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 -- quoted verbatim and unaltered; ShareAlike binds derivatives, which a verbatim quotation is not)
passages.text: If the right upper abdominal quadrant is inaccessible due to traumatic lesions, subcutaneous emphysema, and arm position or without liquid, the examination must proceed to the left upper abdominal quadrant, to search for liquid in the splenorenal space and/or perisplenic. Just as in Region 2, negative FAST is considered absolutely no fluid. Positive FAST is whether small or large amounts of fluid.

passages.source: Savoia P, Jayanthi SK, Chammas MC. Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST). J Med Ultrasound. 2023;31(2):101-6. doi:10.4103/jmu.jmu_12_23 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 -- quoted verbatim and unaltered; ShareAlike binds derivatives, which a verbatim quotation is not)
passages.text: If all regions above are FAST negative and/or inaccessible, the examination must proceed to the pelvis. One practical tip for examining this region is to perform the FAST protocol before bladder catheterization. Performing FAST protocol before it might find the patients bladder full, to be used as an acoustic window for better evaluation of the pelvis. Negative FAST is the absence of fluid. The presence of any quantity of fluid in males constitutes a positive FAST exam. Conversely, females of reproductive age may exhibit physiologically small amounts of fluid in the pouch of Douglas (cul-de-sac). In such cases, a positive FAST result is only established when a large quantity of fluid is observed.

passages.source: Savoia P, Jayanthi SK, Chammas MC. Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST). J Med Ultrasound. 2023;31(2):101-6. doi:10.4103/jmu.jmu_12_23 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 -- quoted verbatim and unaltered; ShareAlike binds derivatives, which a verbatim quotation is not)
passages.text: This should be the first region examined because hemopericardium is potentially more life-threatening than hemoperitoneum or hemothorax. Cardiac tamponade is a cause of cardiac arrest in asystole or pulseless electrical activity. There are two main ways of accessing the pericardial space: subxiphoid and/or anterior left intercostal views. The first one might be limited in patients with higher body mass index, however you may ask for the patient to deeply inspirate and/or use the liver left lobe as an acoustic window, if possible. Negative FAST is considered the absence or a small amount of pericardial fluid, physiological, up to 5 mm wide. A typically positive FAST would be a significant amount of pericardial fluid, responsible to explain the patient shock syndrome.

passages.source: Savoia P, Jayanthi SK, Chammas MC. Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST). J Med Ultrasound. 2023;31(2):101-6. doi:10.4103/jmu.jmu_12_23 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 -- quoted verbatim and unaltered; ShareAlike binds derivatives, which a verbatim quotation is not)
passages.text: The traditional FAST protocol is directed to detect hemopericardium and hemoperitoneum with sensitivity of 85%–96% and specificity more than 98%. Ultrasound, however, achieves 85% sensitivity for intraperitoneal fluid detection only above 150–200 mL. In the context of trauma, fluids in pericardial, peritoneum, or pleural spaces are assumed to be blood until proven otherwise. This logic may lead to false positives once there are situations where fluids other than blood may be present, and ultrasound will not be able to differentiate them, for example, pericarditis, pleural effusions from other conditions, ascites, peritoneal dialysate, ventriculoperitoneal shunt outflow, bladder rupture, ovarian hyperstimulation, ovarian cyst rupture, and massive intravascular volume resuscitation. On the other hand, there are false-negative conditions, where the operator may not be able to detect the bleeding, such as superficial soft-tissue emphysema blocking the ultrasound beam; obese patients, which is a classical limitation for chest and abdominal sonographies; and isolated extraperitoneal injuries. Ultrasound is limited to detect extraperitoneal bleedings, such as an aortic rupture, for example, once the aorta is a retroperitoneal structure. Solid organ injuries are often underdiagnosed or not diagnosed by ultrasound (the numbers are even worse when there is no free fluid), the sensitivity is low, about 40%–63%.

passages.source: Keikha M, Salehi-Marzijarani M, Soldoozi Nejat R, Sheikh Motahar Vahedi H, Mirrezaie SM. Diagnostic Accuracy of Rapid Ultrasound in Shock (RUSH) Exam; A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Bull Emerg Trauma. 2018;6(4):271-8. doi:10.29252/beat-060402 (Creative Commons)
passages.text: The RUSH protocol consists of three steps, in which all three categories of factors (Tank, Pipe, and Pump), which ultimately lead to the occurrence of different types of shock, are examined. Pooled across studies the RUSH exam showed a sensitivity of 0.87 (95% confidence interval 0.80-0.92) and a specificity of 0.98 (95% confidence interval 0.96-0.99). Modest sensitivity and negative likelihood ratio values were obtained for two shock categories, distributive and mixed-etiology, which is likely the most important limitation of applying the RUSH protocol alone to diagnose undifferentiated shock.

passages.source: Ha YR, Toh HC. Clinically integrated multi-organ point-of-care ultrasound for undifferentiated respiratory difficulty, chest pain, or shock: a critical analytic review. J Intensive Care. 2016;4:54. doi:10.1186/s40560-016-0172-1 (CC BY 4.0)
passages.text: Where the lung pattern is not diffusely interstitial, the findings are suggestive of obstructive or hypovolemic shock: IVC plethora indicates obstructive shock, while a small non-plethoric IVC is usually associated with hypovolemic shock. Hypovolemic shock, whether absolute or relative, is the last of the categories to be ruled out, after obstructive and cardiogenic shock have been considered.

passages.source: Ha YR, Toh HC. Clinically integrated multi-organ point-of-care ultrasound for undifferentiated respiratory difficulty, chest pain, or shock: a critical analytic review. J Intensive Care. 2016;4:54. doi:10.1186/s40560-016-0172-1 (CC BY 4.0)
passages.text: Where the lung pattern is diffusely interstitial, cardiogenic shock is most likely. If LV systolic function is impaired, the most likely cause is cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Cardiogenic shock is the second category to be ruled out, after obstructive shock and before absolute or relative hypovolemic shock.

passages.text: Thoracic ultrasound has been increasingly used in the management of patients who visit the emergency department due to acute dyspnea and respiratory failure. Lung ultrasound is applied to pneumothorax, alveolar-interstitial syndrome, pulmonary consolidation, pleural effusion, and to neonates and pediatrics, with robust evidence and strong recommendations. When a normal lung pattern, characterized by a bat sign, A line, and lung sliding, is observed on lung ultrasound, pneumothorax and interstitial syndrome can be excluded.

passages.source: Choi W, Cho YS, Ha YR, et al.; Society Emergency and Critical Care Imaging (SECCI). Role of point-of-care ultrasound in critical care and emergency medicine: update and future perspective. Clin Exp Emerg Med. 2023;10(4):363-81. doi:10.15441/ceem.23.101 (CC BY-NC 4.0)
passages.text: Assessments with focused cardiac ultrasound (FoCUS) can identify several causes in time-sensitive clinical scenarios related to cardiorespiratory symptoms and signs. The five basic views recommended for FoCUS examination include the parasternal long axis, parasternal short axis, apical four chamber, subcostal four chamber, and subcostal inferior vena cava (IVC) views. POCUS can help determine cardiac tamponade, left ventricle failure, pulmonary embolism, hypovolemia, and tension pneumothorax.

passages.source: Choi W, Cho YS, Ha YR, et al.; Society Emergency and Critical Care Imaging (SECCI). Role of point-of-care ultrasound in critical care and emergency medicine: update and future perspective. Clin Exp Emerg Med. 2023;10(4):363-81. doi:10.15441/ceem.23.101 (CC BY-NC 4.0)
passages.text: When a normal lung pattern, characterized by a bat sign, A line, and lung sliding, is observed on lung ultrasound, pneumothorax and interstitial syndrome can be excluded. Focused cardiac ultrasound has limitations in verifying some cardiac conditions such as pericardial fat pads, cysts, preexisting or small pericardial fluid, diastolic dysfunction, valvular diseases, and pulmonary hypertension. Diagnostic usefulness is limited in children, such that a negative extended FAST result in children may not accurately rule out the presence of intra-abdominal injuries.

passages.source: Choi W, Cho YS, Ha YR, et al.; Society Emergency and Critical Care Imaging (SECCI). Role of point-of-care ultrasound in critical care and emergency medicine: update and future perspective. Clin Exp Emerg Med. 2023;10(4):363-81. doi:10.15441/ceem.23.101 (CC BY-NC 4.0)
passages.text: A POCUS study in an intensive care unit is dependent on the skill and experience of the clinician performing the study. Trained physicians should be able to demonstrate proficiency in obtaining and interpreting focused cardiac ultrasound images before performing the examination independently. It is crucial to establish standardized training and education curricula for POCUS in areas such as scope of practice, competency training, hospital credentialing, specialty certification, quality control, and leadership.

passages.source: Choi W, Cho YS, Ha YR, et al.; Society Emergency and Critical Care Imaging (SECCI). Role of point-of-care ultrasound in critical care and emergency medicine: update and future perspective. Clin Exp Emerg Med. 2023;10(4):363-81. doi:10.15441/ceem.23.101 (CC BY-NC 4.0)
passages.text: Comprehensive echocardiography or additional imaging modalities should be considered for a complete evaluation of uncertain findings or complex clinical presentations. Given that POCUS examinations do not cover the full functional and structural status of patients, comprehensive ultrasound has been commonly used in the intensive care unit. Trained physicians should be able to demonstrate proficiency in obtaining and interpreting focused cardiac ultrasound images before performing the examination independently.
